newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain to boost regions' fiscal control - Costa.
newsitem.headline: Spain to boost regions' fiscal control - Costa.

text.p: Spanish Secretary of the Exchequer Juan Costa hit back on Thursday at "irresponsible" criticism of a new regional government financing scheme, saying the new law had vastly improved regions fiscal control.
The new system, which gives regions some control over revenue, is intended to overcome weaknesses of the old system under which regions had responsibility only over expenditures.
"This lack of logic is what we want to resolve," Costa told Reuters in a interview. Now "regions have a very important degree of responsibility."
The government is set to approve a new law designed to give regions more freedom on the budget, allowing them to collect up to 30 percent of income tax within two years.
The law leaves two of Spain's regions with even wider-ranging taxation powers, but some other regions, angered by what they see as privileges, are clamouring for similar status.

"The government will respect its agreement. It won't move a tiny bit. We are happy with the agreement...We do not believe we need to change anything before the five-year pact expires," Costa told Reuters in a interview.
To ask for more is irresponsible, he said.

"I think this shows an extraordinary lack of responsibility. When an agreement has already been reached -- an agreement which was approved by 14 out of the 17 regional governments -- it is not responsible to introduce or to reopen a debate which has already been closed," Costa said.
The centre-right minority government depends on its majority from allies in Catalonia and the Canary Islands.
Catalan leader Jordi Pujol is pushing for a higher degree of autonomy to match the levels enjoyed in the Basque Country and Navarre, whose powers some criticise as privileges.
"To share the responsibility for taxes is not a privilege, it is a responsibility as well," Costa said. Basque and Navarre will also collect "sin taxes" on alcohol and cigarrettes.

But Costa acknowledged that the government's resolve to stick with the pacts "does not keep other political parties from making statements to the media that might be profitable to them from an electoral point of view," Costa said.
"The agreement we reached is intended to be permanent," Costa said. He added the breakdown of 30-70 percent between regions and government in income tax should remain unchanged.
And he said that the agreement was done within the framework of the Constitution.
The opposition Socialist Party (PSOE) said the government should have sought non-partisan support for such a sweeping change in financing.
Costa explained the government has to respect autonomy but it has also to prevent discrimination among different regions.
He said it would oppose, for example, any proposal to raise public workers' salaries after the central government decided to freeze them in order to control expenditure.
He explained that in 1997 the government will have to forge a new agreement in order to coordinate deficit and debt of every single region, putting a ceiling on every one.
A old five-year stability pact will expire the next year. "The regions are well on track," Costa said.
